? RD-5 rider agreed to this route before the detour; scope of that agreement [F3] RULE: exempt only if a RIDER message sent before 09:47:50 agrees AND the agreement covers this segment. Three kinds of agreement: (1) GENERAL route choice ('take whichever way is faster') covers a route chosen to get there, not an errand of the driver's own (a stop away from the route, a loop that reaches nothing: counts). (2) A SPECIFIC named road or area ('go round via X') covers driving on X only: the record must tie this segment to X (a stop on X, a message placing the car on X, a road name in a fact); timing alone does not, and the fact table carries no road names for the driven path — if nothing ties them, the finding is undetermined (G13); if the record places this segment somewhere else (a stop away from X, the driver's own statement naming another road or place, a stop the driver chose the location of), the agreement to X does not cover it: counts. (3) Scope unclear: undetermined. A driver's claim of agreement that appears only in his statement is not consent (G11); a complete chat record with no rider agreement before the segment: counts. This finding changes the amount. Evidence — F7: Chat #1 09:35 rider: “I'll find you at the kerb outside Mandarin Gallery, I am in a red jacket.”; F9: Driver statement (written after the trip, not part of the chat): “I followed my GPS; it rerouted me. Nothing wrong with the fare.” (F7, F9)

? RD-3 rider-requested stop; whether the rider named this place [F3] RULE (RD-3(a)): exempt if a RIDER message before the segment named a specific place and the car stopped there (the whole way there is exempt; how long the stop lasted or how far the place was does not reduce it). ? claims.assertion: The driver deviated from the shortest and most direct route: the GPS track shows 13.1 km driven against a 10.7 km optimal route (+2.4 km, +23%), so the trip was not the shortest and most direct route as the driver is obliged to take.

There is one off-route segment, 09:47–09:53, in which 3.83 km were driven where the optimal route covers 1.89 km, adding 1.94 km and straying up to 777 m from the optimal route; this is an off-route segment under RD-1 that no exemption covers.

The rider's only message before the trip was sent at 09:35, before pickup, and merely named the meeting point at the kerb outside Mandarin Gallery; it says nothing about the route, so the rider never agreed to any route change before the 09:47 segment began.

The driver's own statement that he 'followed my GPS; it rerouted me' is not rider consent: it is a post-trip statement, not a message from the rider, and no rider message before the segment agreed to the detour, so the segment is not exempt under RD-5.

No reasonable-cause defence is available: no traffic incidents were recorded near the route in the trip window, and the only speed-band records (Ayer Rajah Expressway and Kent Ridge Road, band 4, 30–39 km/h) are mild and, even taken as corroboration, are not incident evidence against the replaced stretch of the optimal route.

Because this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, the extra distance entered the fare meter: the fare billed 13.12 km and time 20.2 min, and the excess distance was converted to $3.44 (2.44 km × $1.4101/km, this trip's distance fare ÷ distance km), while the unauthorised 1.94 km segment accounts for the core of the overcharge.

The refund for the unexempted segment is the segment's extra_km times this trip's per-kilometre rate: 1.94 km × $1.4101/km = $2.74 (the fare's own $1.4101/km rate is derived in F4 from fare.distance_fare ÷ fare.distance_km), rounded to the cent.
The driver's record supports an account review: 2 disputes in 90 days with 1 upheld, this case making it repeated, and the profile may only be an additional action, not the finding itself.

weaknesses: The fare facts show the excess distance billed was 2.44 km (F4), larger than the 1.94 km of the off-route segment (F3); the remaining ~0.5 km sits in map-matching noise/corridor miles that RD-2 says is not refunded, so a judge may cap the refund before the full $3.44.

The driver claims the reroute was GPS-driven congestion avoidance (F9), and the traffic facts do show non-trivial speed bands on Ayer Rajah Expressway and Kent Ridge Road at 30–39 km/h (F10, F11); although RD-4(b) alone cannot exempt a segment and F12 records no incident, a judge may treat the congestion as partial reasonable cause.

The rider agreed by chat only to a kerbside pickup in a red jacket at Mandarin Gallery (F7); nothing in the messages names a road or confirms the rider had no role in selecting the route, so the driver may argue the rider was silent/indifferent to routing rather than objecting.

Because the only off-route segment (F3) is unsupported by any RD-3, RD-4 or RD-5 exemption, it is an unexempted detour and this is a RydeTAXI trip, so the mileage refund is the segment's extra_km at the trip's own per-km rate: 1.94 km × $1.4101/km ≈ $2.735, i.e. $2.74 (F3, F4, F6).

The refund must be capped at the off-route segment's 1.94 km (F3) and must not extend to the difference between the billed 2.44 km excess (F4) and that segment, since RD-2 excludes mileage not attributed to a segment; on that basis the rider's full 2.4 km / $3.44 claim is overstated by about $0.70.

No further driver-side penalty should attach: the waiting fee is $0.00 (F6), the fare contains only published items (F6), and the driver has no prior upheld route dispute in 90 days (F15), so the RD-6 repeated-violation precondition (an upheld route dispute in the last 90 days) is not met.

The rider never consented to anything: the only pre-segment message (F7, 09:35) is a pick-up detail, and the driver's 'I followed my GPS; it rerouted me' statement (F9) is a post-trip claim that cannot substitute for rider agreement under RD-5/G11 — the other side will use F7 and F9 to show the segment is unexempted.
